lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you drew Sankey diagrams. A lamp turns 100 J of electricity into 20 J of light. What happens to the other 80 J? (It is wasted, mostly as heat.) Today: power, and paying for energy.
Power is how fast energy is transferred. 1 watt (W) is 1 joule (J) each second; 1 kilowatt (kW) is 1,000 W. Energy = power × time, so a 60 W lamp transfers 60 J every second.
Every appliance has a rating plate that shows its power. Heating jobs use the most: a kettle about 3,000 W and an electric shower about 9,000 W. An LED bulb uses about 10 W.
Bills count energy in kilowatt-hours (kWh), called units. 1 kWh is the energy of 1 kW used for 1 hour. kWh = kW × hours: a 2 kW heater on for 3 hours uses 2 × 3 = 6 kWh.
A home's electricity counter adds up the units used. Take one reading from the next: 12,846 − 12,790 = 56 kWh used this week.
Cost = units × the price of one unit. At 0.25 gold a unit, 56 kWh costs 56 × 0.25 = 14 gold. Most bills add a standing charge too: a fixed amount for each day, however little you use.

Save energy: switch off at the wall, because standby still uses power. An LED bulb uses about 8 W for the light of an old 60 W filament bulb. Boil only the water you need, take shorter showers and wash at 30 °C.

Try it in the world: in Electricity Safety in the LIFE tab, find the adaptor crammed with plugs. A 3 kW kettle alone takes about 13 amps, all a socket can safely give, so too many plugs can overheat. Next: hot and cold reactions.

exercises.prompt: A 60 W lamp is on for 10 seconds. How many joules of energy does it transfer?
exercises.hint: A watt is a joule each second: multiply the watts by the seconds.

exercises.prompt: Which of these uses energy fastest?
exercises.hint: Heating water takes a lot of power: look for the heating job.
exercises.explain: An electric shower uses about 9,000 W; a TV about 100 W, a laptop about 50 W and an LED bulb about 10 W.

exercises.prompt: A 2 kW heater is on for 4 hours. How many kWh does it use?
exercises.explain: 2 × 4 = 8 kWh, or 8 units on the bill.

exercises.prompt: A 1,000 W heater on for 1 hour uses 1 kWh.
exercises.explain: True: 1,000 W = 1 kW, and 1 kW for 1 hour is 1 kWh.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
exercises.hint: Two are about energy, one is about power, and one is about the bill.
exercises.explain: A watt is a joule each second; a joule is a unit of energy; a kilowatt-hour is 1 kW used for 1 hour; a standing charge is a fixed cost for each day.

exercises.prompt: A 1,500 W hair dryer is used for 2 hours in a week. How many kWh is that?
exercises.hint: Change the watts to kilowatts first.

exercises.prompt: A 3 kW kettle boils for 10 minutes in a day. How many kWh does it use?
exercises.hint: Change the minutes to hours: 60 minutes make 1 hour.
exercises.explain: 10 minutes is a sixth of an hour; 3 kW for a sixth of an hour is 3 ÷ 6 = 0.5 kWh.

exercises.prompt: Here are an electricity counter's readings a month apart. How many kWh were used in the month?
exercises.hint: Take the first reading away from the second.

exercises.prompt: A home used 120 kWh, and a unit costs 0.3 gold. What do they cost, in gold?
exercises.hint: Multiply the units by the price of one unit.

exercises.prompt: Sort these habits: do they save energy, or waste it?
items: a long hot shower every day
boiling a full kettle for one cup
exercises.hint: Does each one cut the power or the time, or add to them?
exercises.explain: Switching off at the wall, LED bulbs and washing at 30 °C save energy. Standby, boiling too much water and long hot showers waste it.

exercises.prompt: Why switch a TV off at the wall rather than leave it on standby?
choices: standby still uses power all day
standby uses no power at all
exercises.hint: Is a standby light on? Then something is still using power.
exercises.explain: On standby it still uses a few watts, every hour of the day: over a year that adds up to many kWh.

exercises.prompt: Order these by the energy they use in a day, least first.
exercises.hint: Work out the kWh for each: kW × hours. A big power for a short time can use less.
exercises.explain: LED 0.01 × 5 = 0.05 kWh; TV 0.1 × 4 = 0.4 kWh; kettle 3 kW for a sixth of an hour = 0.5 kWh; shower 9 kW for a sixth of an hour = 1.5 kWh.

exercises.prompt: A 2,000 W heater runs for 3 hours a day for 30 days. A unit costs 0.25 gold. What does that cost, in gold?
exercises.hint: Find the kWh for one day, then for the month, then multiply by the price.

exercises.prompt: A high-power appliance always uses more energy than a low-power one.
exercises.hint: Energy depends on the power and on something else.
exercises.explain: False: energy = power × time. A 3,000 W kettle on for 5 minutes uses 0.25 kWh, less than a 100 W TV on for 4 hours, which uses 0.4 kWh.

exercises.prompt: You swap a 60 W bulb for an 8 W LED and use it 5 hours a day for 100 days. How many kWh do you save?
exercises.hint: Find the watts saved, multiply by all the hours, then change watt-hours to kWh.

exercises.prompt: A home heats its water with electricity. Which change would save the most energy?
choices: a laptop instead of a TV
exercises.hint: Look for the job that uses the most power for the longest time.
exercises.explain: An electric shower uses about 9,000 W, far more than the others, so cutting its time saves the most energy.
